name: Sandia National Laboratories

profile.address: 880A, K South Avenue Southeast, Bernalillo County, New Mexico, 87116
profile.reading: This facility in Bernalillo County, New Mexico, is a high performance computing site operated by Sandia National Laboratories, whose main New Mexico campus sits on Kirtland Air Force Base in Albuquerque and employs more than 12,000 people. Sandia is a United States federal research laboratory, owned by the government but managed under contract, currently by National Technology and Engineering Solutions of Sandia, a wholly owned subsidiary of Honeywell International, a management contract that began in May 2017. It is one of three national laboratories run under the Department of Energy's National Nuclear Security Administration, alongside Los Alamos and Lawrence Livermore, and its mission centers on nuclear weapons stewardship, nonproliferation, arms control support and broader national security science, work organized across multiple technical areas on the Kirtland site. Sandia's Center for Computing Research develops the computer system architecture, both hardware and software, along with the computational physical simulation and data and decision science capability that underpin this mission, describing its work as addressing some of the nation's most demanding national security computing challenges and explicitly referencing exascale class computing among its research goals. High performance computing at Sandia traces back through machines such as the ASCI Red system of the late 1990s, an early terascale computer built for the Accelerated Strategic Computing Initiative, through to more recent large scale systems the laboratory has fielded for stockpile stewardship simulation, weapons physics modeling and broader defense science computing. Because this work supports classified and sensitive national security missions, Sandia does not publish the kind of commercial specifications, such as leasable floor area or power capacity available to tenants, that describe a colocation data center. What is publicly documented is the laboratory's role, its ownership and management structure, and a general history of fielding some of the country's most capable government owned research computers in support of the Department of Energy's nuclear security mission, rather than any commercial hosting business. Facilities of this kind require electrical power and cooling infrastructure on a scale comparable to large commercial data centers simply to keep thousands of processors and accelerators running continuously, even though the laboratory does not publish those figures the way a commercial colocation provider would, since Sandia's computing is built to support its own mission rather than to be leased out, and detailed capacity numbers are treated as programmatic rather than public information.

reading:
Sandia National Laboratories is a Department of Energy and National Nuclear Security Administration laboratory in Albuquerque, New Mexico, managed and operated by National Technology and Engineering Solutions of Sandia, a Honeywell subsidiary, under an NNSA management and operating contract. It is in this registry as a government operator, and the reason a weapons laboratory runs its own data centre rather than buying colocation is straightforward. Much of the work is classified or export controlled, the machines are one off procurements that no commercial hall is built to host, and the computing exists to serve nuclear stockpile stewardship and national security engineering rather than any external customer.

The registry's New Mexico row corresponds to Sandia's high performance computing facility on the Albuquerque campus, and here the public record is unusually good, because the Department of Energy published the building as an efficiency case study. Building 725E was completed in October 2018 and joined to 725W, which dates from 2005. It is about 14,000 square feet and was designed for 14 megawatts of IT load at full build out. That figure is worth flagging as one of the few in this registry that genuinely is critical IT load rather than utility service, because it comes from a federal design study rather than from a directory or a marketing page. It earned LEED version 4 Gold under the building design and construction rating for data centres, certified roughly fourteen months after completion and the first certification under Sandia's LEED version 4 campus programme.

The cooling design is the point of the case study. The building runs three water loops at different temperatures, a process water loop supplying around 76 degrees Fahrenheit for direct liquid cooled racks, a medium temperature loop near 60 degrees and a chilled water loop near 58 degrees, and it rejects heat in order of cost, thermosyphon dry coolers first, then evaporative cooling towers, then mechanical chillers. New Mexico's dry air lets an airside economiser carry roughly 75 to 80 per cent of hours without mechanical cooling, with the hall held near 78 degrees. Sandia reported that the thermosyphon saved more than half a million gallons of water in its first six months, and that later operational tuning saved a further 200,000 gallons a year and about 63,000 dollars a year in chiller energy. A dedicated 250 kilowatt photovoltaic array serves the facility, which is on site generation rather than either standby power or IT capacity.

The named machines give a sense of what fills that envelope. Astra, deployed in 2018, was among the first large Arm processor systems to reach the Top500 list and draws about 1.2 megawatts. Attaway runs at roughly 600 kilowatts and Manzano at roughly 720 kilowatts, and Yacumama was relocated into the building in 2019. Sandia also operates a Livermore, California site that this New Mexico registry row does not cover, and no aggregate laboratory wide megawatt figure is published or estimated here. The 14 megawatt design capacity of 725E is a building specification, not a statement of what Sandia currently draws.
